<reason>B won the decisive clash: every CON harm (unmonitored meds, uncontested claims, the 3 a.m. hallway) presupposes a patient who enters treatment, and B showed the disclosure default is what blocks entry. The turning point was A's own claim in Rebuttal 2 that the sickest patients "do not self-refer under any billing regime" — B's closing converted this into a boomerang: confidential billing then costs CON none of the severe cases (the noticing happens in the home, not the mailbox), while the disclosure default additionally loses the treatable self-referrers. A's closing response (downstream monitoring blindness) was clever but weak — in-home observers don't need EOBs to keep observing, and A never engaged B's Rebuttal 2 answer that clinicians provide safety-planning, follow-up, and intact duty-to-warn in treatment. A also sidestepped B's Q1 (the opt-in protects only patients who already arrived), had its R1 clipped for length, and dropped its best surviving point (the appeals/standing problem) in its own closing. A's available-vs-default distinction and "concealment is the illness" were genuinely strong, but B stayed closer to the motion's text (blocking *automatic* revelation), answered both pressure questions directly, and made the debate easier to decide.</reason>
<best_rebuttal>B's closing exploitation of A4.3's concession that severe patients arrive via family "under any billing regime" — this collapsed CON's weighing, since the "eyes in the home" don't depend on billing, leaving disclosure with only costs (deterred self-referrers) and no offsetting gain; paired with B4.1's clean answer that suspicion carries strictly less information than an EOB, it sealed the round.</best_rebuttal>
